Sunlight looks white because it contains all visible wavelengths, from violet and blue to red. When this light enters Earth’s atmosphere, it encounters molecules of nitrogen and oxygen that are much smaller than the wavelengths of visible light. This causes Rayleigh scattering, in which light is redirected by these tiny particles. The key feature of Rayleigh scattering is that it is much stronger for shorter wavelengths: its intensity is roughly proportional to \(1/\lambda^4\), where \(\lambda\) is wavelength. So blue and violet light are scattered far more efficiently than green, yellow, or red light.

Because blue light is scattered so strongly in all directions, it reaches our eyes from every part of the sky, not just from the direction of the Sun. When you look away from the Sun, you are mostly seeing sunlight that has been bounced around by air molecules. Although violet light is scattered even more than blue, the Sun emits less violet, some of it is absorbed in the upper atmosphere, and human eyes are less sensitive to violet than to blue. The combined result is that the sky appears blue rather than violet.

Rayleigh scattering also explains why the sky changes color at sunrise and sunset. When the Sun is low, its light travels through much more atmosphere before reaching you. The blue light is scattered away along that long path, while red and orange light, which scatter less, are more likely to pass through directly.
